idiom_name: struct/class conforming to the collaborator protocol with canned returns
implementation_notes: Swift's realization is a protocol for the collaborator plus a test-only struct that conforms to it and returns the canned value; XCTest supplies assertions and expectations but no doubles, and pure Swift has no dynamic method interception, so nothing is configured at runtime - the compiler checks conformance and initializer injection is the seam. Keep the double in the test target, inject it through a protocol-typed property or initializer parameter, and cover async collaborators by marking the test async (or with XCTestExpectation) while the stub answers immediately. Macro-based generators (SwiftMocking, Sourcery templates) can emit the same conformance when the protocol is wide; for one canned answer the hand-written type is clearer and needs no toolchain support.
pitfalls: A protocol with many requirements forces the stub to implement or trap in all of them; split the protocol or provide default implementations in an extension.
A struct stub injected by value is copied, so a test that wants to observe what the SUT did must use a reference type or a class wrapper.
Stub answers arrive instantly, which hides MainActor/actor-isolation requirements; annotate the test or the double, or the assertion runs off the expected actor.

variants.name: Macro-generated mock type (SwiftMocking, Sourcery)
variants.implementation_notes: Swift 5.9 introduced macros, and tooling such as SwiftMocking uses them to generate a mock type from the collaborator protocol: the test writes when(mock.price(for: "apple")).thenReturn(13) for the canned answer and optionally verify(...) for the interaction, with test-scoped isolation so the stubs are reset between tests. Sourcery-based templates generate a plain conforming type instead, which works on older toolchains but offers no stubbing DSL. Choose a generator when the protocol is wide (hand-writing every member is noise) or the team already runs the plugin; the generated mock is the library counterpart of the hand-written protocol conformance and both can coexist - generate the wide protocols, hand-write the small ones.
pitfalls: Macro expansion requires the Swift 5.9 toolchain and a build plugin or package macro; projects on older Xcodes must fall back to the hand-written conformance.
The generated mock lives in the test target and must be regenerated when the protocol changes; a stale mock compiles against the old shape and hides the drift.
A generated mock's unimplemented members trap or fail on unexpected calls, so every member the SUT touches needs a programmed answer - the generation saves typing, not configuration.
